{{Short description|Russian-American mathematician (1946–2018)}}
'''Victor  Lomonosov''' (7 February 1946 &ndash; 29 March 2018) was a Russian-American [[mathematician]] known for his work in [[functional analysis]]. In [[operator theory]], he is best known for his work in 1973 on the [[invariant subspace|invariant subspace problem]], which was described by  [[Walter Rudin]] in his classical book on Functional Analysis as "[[Lomonosov's invariant subspace theorem|Lomonosov's spectacular invariant subspace theorem]]".<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/RudinW.FunctionalAnalysis2e1991|title=Functional Analysis|last=Rudin|first=Walter|publisher=McGraw-Hill|year=1991|isbn=0-07-100944-2|edition=2nd|location=New York|orig-year=1973}}</ref>  Lomonosov gives a very short proof, using the [[Schauder fixed point theorem]], that if a bounded linear operator ''T'' on a [[Banach space]] commutes with a non-zero [[compact operator]] then ''T'' has a non-trivial invariant subspace.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Lomonosov | first1=V. I. | title=Invariant subspaces of the family of operators that commute with a completely continuous operator | mr=0420305 | year=1973 | journal=Funktsional'nyi Analiz i Ego Prilozheniya | volume=7 | issue=3 | pages=55–56}}<br/>
:Translated in {{cite journal |last1=Lomonosov |first1=V. I. |title=Invariant subspaces for the family of operators which commute with a completely continuous operator |journal=Functional Analysis and Its Applications |date=1973 |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=213–214 |doi=10.1007/BF01080698}}</ref>   Lomonosov has also published on the [[Bishop–Phelps theorem]]<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Lomonosov|first1=Victor|title=A counterexample to the Bishop-Phelps theorem in complex spaces|journal=[[Israel Journal of Mathematics]]|date=2000|volume=115|pages=25–28|doi=10.1007/bf02810578|doi-access=|s2cid=53646715}}</ref> and Burnside's Theorem.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Lomonosov|first1=Victor|title=An extension of Burnside's theorem to infinite-dimensional spaces|journal=[[Israel Journal of Mathematics]]|date=1991|volume=75|issue=2–3|pages=329–339|doi=10.1007/bf02776031|doi-access=|s2cid=120120695}}</ref>

Lomonosov received his master's degree from [[Moscow State University]] in 1969 and his Ph.D. from the [[National University of Kharkiv]] in 1974  (adviser [[Vladimir Matsaev]]). He was appointed as an Associate Professor at [[Kent State University]] in the fall of 1991 and was promoted to Professor at the same university in 1999.
